title: Introduction to Blockchain & Web3
tagline: See how blockchains work, hands-on: break a chain, mine a block and judge real projects
summary: A first course in blockchain and Web3 with live labs: hash text and watch the avalanche effect, tamper with a chain and re-mine it, calculate fees and Bitcoin's supply, and learn how to judge claims and stay safe. No coding or account is needed.

modules.title: Why blockchain exists
modules.summary: The problem of trust in shared records, and the simple idea of a ledger that many people keep together.
modules.outcome: You can explain the trust problem, describe centralised and distributed ledgers and say what a blockchain adds.
modules.intro: Every time money moves, a land is sold or a certificate is issued, someone has to keep a record and everyone else has to trust it. Blockchain is a different way of keeping that record. To appreciate it, start with the problem it was invented to solve.

topics.title: The trust problem
topics.html:
When you pay a friend with a bank app, the bank subtracts money from your account and adds it to theirs. You do not check the arithmetic; you trust the bank to keep an honest record. This works well most of the time, but it means everything depends on one keeper being honest, competent, secure and always available.

What can go wrong with a single keeper
RiskExample
MistakesA clerk enters the wrong amount and nobody notices for years
DishonestyAn insider quietly changes a record for gain
HackingOne database breached and thousands of records altered or stolen
CensorshipA keeper refuses to process a payment or freezes an account
OutageThe server is down so nobody can use the record
Definition

Double spending. Using the same digital money twice. With physical cash it is impossible because the note leaves your hand. With digital files it is easy, because copying costs nothing, so digital money needs a keeper to say 'this coin has already been spent'.

Before 2008 every digital payment system solved double spending by having a central keeper such as a bank, a card network or a payment company. Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 paper on Bitcoin asked: can a network of strangers keep one honest record of who owns what, with no central keeper? The answer, combining several older ideas, was the blockchain.

Check what you just learned

1. What problem does 'double spending' describe?
  • Paying twice for the same item by mistake
  • Two people sharing one wallet
  • Using the same digital money more than once (correct)
  • Charging fees twice

Digital files copy easily, so something must stop the same coin being spent twice.

Tip

Whenever you meet a new technology claim, ask: who is the keeper of the record, and what happens if they fail or cheat?

Check what you just learned

1. In a traditional bank system, who prevents double spending?
  • The customers
  • A blockchain
  • Nobody
  • The central bank or payment company that keeps the record (correct)

A central keeper updates one authoritative record.

2. Which is a risk of a single keeper?
  • One failure or one dishonest insider can corrupt or block the record (correct)
  • Everyone can see the record
  • Records are always public
  • Transactions are instant

Concentrated trust is concentrated risk.
keyPoints: Most records rely on one trusted keeper.
Double spending is the core problem of digital money.

topics.title: From ledgers to shared ledgers
topics.html:
Definition

Ledger. A record of transactions: who paid whom, what was bought, what is owed. Accountants have kept ledgers for thousands of years.

Three ways of keeping a ledger
TypeWho keeps itWho trusts whomExample
CentralisedOne organisationEveryone trusts the keeperA bank's account database
Decentralised copies of one record with a leaderSeveral organisations, one of which leadsMembers trust the leaderA banking consortium run by one operator
DistributedMany independent participants each hold a full copyParticipants trust the rules and the maths, not each otherBitcoin and Ethereum

In a distributed ledger every participant, called a node, keeps a full copy and checks every new entry against the rules before accepting it. If one copy is altered, it no longer matches the others and is rejected. Cheating requires fooling most of the network at the same time.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a blockchain is simply 'a database'. It is a database that many parties write to under shared rules, with a very different set of trade-offs.
  • Thinking decentralised means anonymous. Most public chains are pseudonymous: addresses are public, even if names are not attached.

Check what you just learned

1. A node is:
  • A type of coin
  • A computer that keeps a copy of the ledger and checks new entries (correct)
  • A bank
  • A password

Nodes are the participants.
keyPoints: A distributed ledger is kept by many nodes that check each other.
Trust moves from a keeper to rules and maths.

topics.title: What a blockchain is
topics.html:
Definition

Blockchain. A distributed ledger in which transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block contains a cryptographic fingerprint (a hash) of the block before it, so the blocks form a chain. Altering an old block changes its fingerprint and breaks every link after it.

Try the lab below. Each block stores its data, a number called a nonce and the hash of the previous block. Change any block's data and watch what happens to it and to the blocks that come after it.

Break the chain, then repair it

Edit the data in Block 2. Then press 'Re-link and mine' on each red block in order to make the chain valid again.

A chain of 4 linked blocks. Change the data in one block and see every later block break until it is mined again.

Repairing the chain needed work: every later block had to be mined again. On a real network that work would have to be done faster than all the honest nodes are adding new blocks, which is why rewriting history is practically impossible once a block is buried under many others.

Parts of a block
PartPurpose
Data (transactions)What happened
Previous hashLinks to the block before it
NonceA number miners change until the block's hash meets the network's target
HashThe fingerprint of the whole block
TimestampWhen the block was created

Check what you just learned

1. If you change the data in an old block, what happens?
  • Nothing, the chain ignores it
  • Only that block is deleted
  • Its hash changes, so the next block's link no longer matches (correct)
  • The network gives it a new date

The change ripples through every later link.

Check what you just learned

1. Each block stores the hash of:
  • The next block
  • The miner's name
  • The user's password
  • The previous block (correct)

That is what links them.

Key terms: flip and sort

Ledger
A record of transactions
Node
A computer that keeps a copy and checks entries
Block
A group of transactions with a link to the previous block
Hash
A fixed-length fingerprint of data
Double spending
Using the same digital money twice
Distributed
Kept by many independent participants
keyPoints: A blockchain links blocks with hashes.
Changing history breaks the chain.

modules.title: How it works
modules.summary: Hashes, signatures and consensus: the three ideas that make a blockchain trustworthy.
modules.outcome: You can explain hashing, public and private keys and how a network agrees on one history.
modules.intro: A blockchain looks magical until you see its parts. This module takes the three key ideas one at a time, with labs you can play with: hashing makes tampering visible, signatures prove who authorised a payment, and consensus makes strangers agree.

topics.title: Hashing: digital fingerprints
topics.html:
Definition

Hash function. A function that turns any input into a fixed-length output called a hash or digest. The same input always gives the same hash, but a tiny change gives a completely different one, and nobody can work backwards from the hash to the input.

Bitcoin and many other chains use SHA-256, which produces a 256-bit hash, usually written as 64 hexadecimal digits. Type below and watch the fingerprint change.

Try SHA-256

Change one letter and watch how much of the hash changes.

Type any text and see its SHA-256 fingerprint change completely when one letter changes.

Four properties that matter
PropertyMeaningWhy a blockchain needs it
DeterministicSame input, same outputEveryone can recompute and compare
Fast to computeHashing is quickNodes can check blocks easily
One-wayYou cannot recover the input from the hashFingerprints can be shared safely
Avalanche effectA tiny change flips about half the bitsTampering cannot be hidden
Collision resistantIt is practically impossible to find two inputs with the same hashA fingerprint identifies exactly one block

Check what you just learned

1. You change one letter of a message. The new hash will be:
  • Completely different (correct)
  • Almost the same as before
  • Shorter
  • Identical

That is the avalanche effect.

Tip

A hash is not encryption. You cannot 'decrypt' a hash; you can only guess inputs and check whether they produce the same hash.

Check what you just learned

1. Which property makes tampering visible?
  • It is secret
  • A tiny change gives a completely different hash (correct)
  • It is slow
  • It can be reversed

The avalanche effect exposes edits.

2. A hash of 64 hexadecimal digits corresponds to how many bits?
  • 64
  • 128
  • 256 (correct)
  • 512

Each hex digit is 4 bits.
keyPoints: A hash is a fingerprint: deterministic, one-way and sensitive to tiny changes.
SHA-256 gives a 256-bit result.

topics.title: Keys and signatures
topics.html:
To move money you must prove that you own it without handing over a password that others could reuse. Blockchains use public-key cryptography for this: every user has a pair of keys that are mathematically linked.

The key pair
KeyWho knows itWhat it does
Private keyOnly youCreates signatures; must never be shared
Public keyEveryoneLets anyone verify that a signature was made by the matching private key
AddressEveryoneA shorter identifier derived from the public key, where funds are sent

Because the signature depends on both the exact transaction and your private key, nobody can change the amount or recipient after signing, and nobody can sign for you without the key. A wallet is software or a device that stores your private keys and signs for you; it does not 'hold coins'. The coins are records on the blockchain, which your key lets you move.

Watch out

Whoever holds your private key, or the recovery phrase that generates it, controls your funds, and a blockchain transaction cannot be reversed by a bank. There is no 'forgot password' button.

Check what you just learned

1. What lets other people verify that you authorised a payment?
  • Your private key
  • Your hash
  • Your phone number
  • Your public key and your signature (correct)

The public key checks the signature.

Check what you just learned

1. Which key must never be shared?
  • Private key (correct)
  • Public key
  • Address
  • Hash

It controls your funds.
keyPoints: Private keys sign, public keys verify.
A wallet stores keys; it does not store coins.

topics.title: Consensus: agreeing without a boss
topics.html:
If thousands of nodes each receive transactions in a slightly different order, how do they agree on one history? The answer is a consensus mechanism: a set of rules that decides who may add the next block and how everyone else accepts it.

Two main families
MechanismWho adds blocksHow it resists cheatingExamples
Proof of Work (PoW)Miners who find a nonce so that the block's hash meets a difficult targetCheating needs more computing power than the honest majority, which costs real energy and moneyBitcoin
Proof of Stake (PoS)Validators chosen in proportion to the coins they lock up as a depositDishonest validators can lose part of their deposit (slashing)Ethereum since 2022

Feel the work in proof of work

Raise the difficulty and mine a block: each extra zero makes the search about 16 times longer on average.

A chain of 3 linked blocks. Change the data in one block and see every later block break until it is mined again.

Formula · Expected tries for PoW

expected tries ≈ 16 ^ (number of leading zero hex digits)

With 3 leading zeros you need about 16³ = 4,096 tries on average.

What consensus has to achieve

  • Agreement: every honest node ends up with the same history.
  • Liveness: new valid transactions keep being added.
  • Security: it is very costly to rewrite the past or to add invalid transactions.
  • Openness: anyone who follows the rules can take part.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is rewriting history so costly on a proof-of-work chain?
  • Because of a legal ban
  • You must redo the work for the changed block and every block after it (correct)
  • Because blocks are secret
  • Because blocks are large

Work, not permission, protects the past.

Check what you just learned

1. In proof of stake, validators are discouraged from cheating because they:
  • Are paid nothing
  • Must use more electricity
  • Can lose part of their staked deposit (correct)
  • Are anonymous

Slashing makes cheating costly.

Key terms: flip and sort

Hash function
Turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint
SHA-256
A widely used 256-bit hash function
Private key
A secret that signs transactions
Public key
Shared key used to verify signatures
Wallet
Software or hardware that stores keys and signs
Consensus
How a network agrees on one history
Proof of work
Consensus by computing work
Proof of stake
Consensus by locked deposits
keyPoints: Consensus lets strangers agree on one history.
PoW uses computing work; PoS uses locked deposits.

modules.title: Bitcoin and Ethereum
modules.summary: The first working blockchain, and the one that made blockchains programmable.
modules.outcome: You can describe how Bitcoin works, what Ethereum adds with smart contracts and how other chains and layers fit in.
modules.intro: Two systems shaped the field. Bitcoin proved that digital money without a central keeper could work. Ethereum asked whether the same shared computer could run programs, not just keep a list of payments.

topics.title: Bitcoin in one page
topics.html:
Bitcoin launched in January 2009 after a white paper published under the name Satoshi Nakamoto in 2008. It is a network of nodes that keep a ledger of payments in its own unit, bitcoin (BTC). New blocks arrive on average every ten minutes, and miners who add them earn newly created coins plus transaction fees.

Key facts
FactDetail
ConsensusProof of work with SHA-256
Block timeAbout 10 minutes on average
SupplyCapped at 21 million coins
IssuanceNew coins come as the block reward, which halves about every four years (every 210,000 blocks)
ModelUnspent transaction outputs (UTXOs): coins are like banknotes of exact sizes that you spend whole and get change from

How supply grows

Change the number of halvings that have happened to see the reward and the coins created so far (a simplified model: 210,000 blocks per era, starting at 50 coins).

Adjust Halvings so far and see Current reward per block, Coins created so far change.

Bitcoin is deliberately simple and conservative. Its scripting is limited, which keeps it easier to secure but means it is mainly used as a store of value and a payment network rather than a platform for applications.

Check what you just learned

1. How many bitcoins will ever exist, according to the protocol rules?
  • 1 million
  • No limit
  • 100 million
  • 21 million (correct)

The cap is built into the rules.

Watch out

Anything about prices, mining rewards after the current period, or regulation changes over time. Treat figures in articles as dated and check an up-to-date source.

Check what you just learned

1. Roughly how often does a new Bitcoin block arrive?
  • Every 10 minutes (correct)
  • Every second
  • Every hour
  • Every day

The difficulty adjusts to keep that average.
keyPoints: Bitcoin is a proof-of-work ledger of payments with a 21 million cap.
Block rewards halve every 210,000 blocks.

topics.title: Ethereum and smart contracts
topics.html:
Ethereum, proposed by Vitalik Buterin and launched in 2015, generalised the idea. Instead of only recording payments, its blockchain can store and run small programs called smart contracts. Anyone can deploy one, and anyone can call it; the network executes the code and every node agrees on the result.

Definition

Smart contract. A program stored on a blockchain that runs exactly as written when it is called. Once deployed, its code is public and, unless it is designed to be upgradable, cannot be changed.

Bitcoin versus Ethereum (simplified)
BitcoinEthereum
Main purposeDigital money and store of valueA programmable shared computer
Native coinBTCETH (used to pay fees)
ProgramsVery limited scriptsSmart contracts in languages such as Solidity
ConsensusProof of workProof of stake since September 2022 (the Merge)
FeesPer byte of dataPer unit of computation, called gas
Worked example

A simple smart contract idea

Two friends bet 100 rupees on a match and use a contract to hold the money.

  1. Both send their stake to the contract.
  2. After the match, an agreed data source reports the winner.
  3. The contract sends 200 rupees to the winner automatically.
  4. No friend or middleman can run away with the money.

Answer. The contract replaces the trusted middleman with code, provided the data source is honest.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is true of smart contracts?
  • They are legal documents lawyers must approve
  • They are programs that run on the blockchain as written (correct)
  • They only work on Bitcoin
  • They can never hold money

Code is the contract.

Check what you just learned

1. Ethereum moved from proof of work to proof of stake in:
  • 2009
  • 2015
  • 2022 (correct)
  • 2030

The Merge happened in September 2022.
keyPoints: Ethereum adds programmable smart contracts.
Fees on Ethereum are paid in gas, priced in ETH.

topics.title: Other chains and layers
topics.html:
Public blockchains face a trilemma: it is hard to be at once decentralised, secure and fast. Different projects choose different trade-offs, and a whole ecosystem has grown around the problem.

Common categories
CategoryIdeaExamples (illustrative)
Layer 1A base blockchain with its own consensusBitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Avalanche
Layer 2A system built on top of a layer 1 that batches many transactions and posts proof to it, to be cheaper and fasterRollups on Ethereum
SidechainA separate chain connected by a bridge, with its own securityVarious
Private or permissioned chainOnly approved participants take partEnterprise systems such as Hyperledger Fabric

Questions to ask about any chain

  1. Who validates blocks and how many independent parties are there?
  2. How much does a transaction cost, and how fast is it final?
  3. How much has it been tested and audited?
  4. What would happen if its main developers vanished?
  5. How do assets move between this chain and others, and how safe are the bridges?
Watch out

Bridges between chains have been one of the most attacked parts of the ecosystem. Moving funds across a bridge adds risk.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a layer 2 do?
  • Replaces the base chain
  • Mines coins
  • Stores private data
  • Batches transactions and relies on a layer 1 for security (correct)

It inherits security while cutting cost.

Check what you just learned

1. A permissioned blockchain is one where:
  • Only approved participants can take part (correct)
  • Anyone can join
  • There are no blocks
  • Nothing is recorded

Enterprise networks often work this way.

Key terms: flip and sort

Bitcoin
The first blockchain, a payment network
Ethereum
A programmable blockchain
Smart contract
A program stored and run on a blockchain
Gas
Fee unit for computation on Ethereum
Layer 2
A network built on a base chain to scale it
Permissioned
Only approved participants
keyPoints: Chains trade off decentralisation, security and speed.
Layer 2s scale a layer 1; bridges add risk.

modules.title: Web3 in practice
modules.summary: Wallets, apps, tokens and fees: what using Web3 actually involves.
modules.outcome: You can describe how people use wallets and decentralised apps, distinguish coins from tokens and estimate transaction fees.
modules.intro: Web3 is the label for internet services built on blockchains, where users hold their own keys and assets instead of logging in to a company account. This module shows what that means in daily use.

topics.title: Wallets and decentralised apps
topics.html:
Web2 and Web3 compared
Web2 appWeb3 app (dApp)
IdentityEmail and password held by the companyA wallet address you control
Data and assetsStored in the company's databaseAssets on a public chain; some data off-chain
RulesSet and changed by the companyOften encoded in smart contracts anyone can read
If the company disappearsYour account is goneYour assets may still exist, if the contracts do
PaymentsCard networks and banksDirectly in tokens

A dApp's website is usually an ordinary web page. What makes it a dApp is that it reads from and writes to smart contracts on a blockchain through your wallet. The page can be shut down while the contracts keep running, but a convincing fake page can also trick you, so checking addresses matters.

Custodial and non-custodial wallets

  • Custodial: a company such as an exchange holds the keys for you, like a bank. Easier, but you trust the company.
  • Non-custodial: you hold the keys. You control the assets, but you are responsible for backups and for avoiding scams.
  • Hardware wallets keep keys in a dedicated device that signs transactions without exposing the key to your computer.

Check what you just learned

1. In a non-custodial wallet, who is responsible for the keys?
  • The exchange
  • The user (correct)
  • The miners
  • The government

Self-custody means self-responsibility.

Check what you just learned

1. A dApp is best described as:
  • An app that only works offline
  • A video game
  • An app whose logic runs partly on smart contracts and uses your wallet (correct)
  • A bank website

The chain holds the logic and assets.
keyPoints: dApps use a wallet instead of a password login.
Custodial wallets trade control for convenience.

topics.title: Coins, tokens and NFTs
topics.html:
The vocabulary
TermMeaningExample
CoinThe native currency of a blockchain, used to pay fees and secure itBTC on Bitcoin, ETH on Ethereum
TokenAn asset created by a smart contract on an existing chainA stablecoin or a game currency
FungibleEach unit is interchangeableRupee notes; ERC-20 tokens
Non-fungible (NFT)Each unit is uniqueA digital collectible, a ticket or a certificate
StablecoinA token designed to track a stable value such as a currencyA token backed by reserves

Tokens can represent many things: money, shares in a project, access rights, loyalty points or ownership of a digital item. What a token represents in law depends on the country and the design, and regulators in many places treat some tokens as securities.

Watch out

A token existing does not mean it has value, or that the promises made about it will be kept. Many tokens have collapsed or were fraudulent. Never invest money you cannot afford to lose.

Check what you just learned

1. An NFT is:
  • A coin every unit of which is identical
  • A type of fee
  • A kind of wallet
  • A token where each unit is unique (correct)

Non-fungible means not interchangeable.

Check what you just learned

1. ETH on Ethereum is a:
  • Native coin used for fees (correct)
  • Token created by a contract
  • NFT
  • Wallet

Native coins pay for network use.
keyPoints: Coins belong to a chain; tokens are made by contracts.
NFTs are unique, fungible tokens are interchangeable.

topics.title: Fees, speed and finality
topics.html:
Every transaction competes for limited space in the next block, so busy networks cost more. On Ethereum, the fee is the gas used by the transaction multiplied by the gas price, which is quoted in gwei (one billionth of an ETH).

Formula · Fee on Ethereum

fee = gas used × gas price

A simple transfer uses 21,000 gas. At 30 gwei the fee is 630,000 gwei, or 0.00063 ETH.

Fee calculator

Change gas used, gas price and the price of ETH to see the fee. The ETH price here is a teaching figure, not a quote.

Adjust Gas used, Gas price (gwei), Price of 1 ETH (rupees) and see Fee in ETH, Fee in rupees change.

Definition

Finality. The point after which a transaction is, for practical purposes, permanent. On some chains a transaction is only probably final after several more blocks, so exchanges often wait for a number of confirmations.

Practical habits

  • Check the network fee before you confirm.
  • Send a small test transaction first when using a new address.
  • Avoid sending when the network is unusually busy, unless it is urgent.
  • Make sure you are on the right network: sending to the right address on the wrong chain can lose funds.

Check what you just learned

1. A simple Ethereum transfer uses about:
  • 1 gas
  • 21,000 gas (correct)
  • 21 million gas
  • No gas

The standard cost of a basic transfer.

Key terms: flip and sort

dApp
An application using smart contracts and a wallet
Custodial
A third party holds your keys
Token
An asset created by a smart contract
NFT
A unique token
Stablecoin
A token designed to hold a stable value
Gwei
A billionth of an ETH, used to quote gas prices
keyPoints: Fees depend on demand and on the work a transaction needs.
Finality is when a transaction is practically permanent.

modules.title: Use cases and limits
modules.summary: Where blockchains help, where they do not, and how to judge a claim.
modules.outcome: You can judge whether a project truly needs a blockchain, name real use cases and explain the main limits.
modules.intro: Between hype and scepticism there is a practical middle: blockchains are a useful tool for some problems and a poor one for many others. This module teaches you to tell which is which.

topics.title: Where blockchains help
topics.html:
Typical use cases
AreaHow a shared ledger helpsTypical concern
Payments and remittancesMoves value across borders without several intermediariesRegulation, volatility, on and off ramps
Supply chainsShared record of a product's journey among companies that do not fully trust each otherData entered by people may be wrong
Digital identity and credentialsVerifiable certificates held by the ownerPrivacy and recovery
Finance (DeFi)Open lending and trading through smart contractsSmart contract bugs and scams
Digital ownershipVerifiable ownership of digital items and ticketsLegal meaning of ownership
Public records and auditsTamper-evident logs anyone can checkWhat to put on a public chain

The most successful uses share a pattern: several parties need to share data, nobody wants to hand control of that data to one of them, and a tamper-evident history matters.

Check what you just learned

1. Which pattern suggests a blockchain may help?
  • One company controls everything
  • Data is private and for one user
  • Several parties who do not fully trust each other need a shared record (correct)
  • Speed is the only goal

Shared control with tamper evidence is the sweet spot.

Tip

Ask: 'Who are the writers, who are the readers, and why can they not simply use a database run by one of them?' If there is a good answer, a blockchain may be justified.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is most likely to need a blockchain?
  • A personal to-do list
  • A private notebook
  • A single school's timetable
  • A shared record among competing companies (correct)

Multiple untrusting parties.
keyPoints: Blockchains suit shared records among parties that do not fully trust each other.
Always ask why a normal database would not do.

topics.title: Limits and trade-offs
topics.html:
Honest limits
LimitExplanation
Garbage in, garbage outA blockchain proves that data was recorded and not changed; it cannot prove the data was true when entered. Connecting real-world facts to the chain needs trusted sources called oracles
ScalabilityMany nodes must repeat the same work, so throughput is lower than a centralised database
CostFees and engineering effort can exceed the value for simple problems
Immutability cuts both waysMistakes and illegal content are hard to remove; privacy rules such as the right to erasure can conflict with permanent records
Energy useProof-of-work chains use large amounts of electricity; proof of stake uses far less
User experienceManaging keys and fees is hard for beginners
RegulationRules for tokens, exchanges and taxes differ by country and are still changing

Good engineers consider these trade-offs before choosing a technology. A cheerful claim that 'blockchain solves everything' is a warning sign, not a recommendation.

Common mistakes

  • Putting personal data directly on a public blockchain.
  • Assuming that a record on a blockchain must be true.
  • Ignoring legal advice about tokens and data protection.

Check what you just learned

1. Why can't a blockchain by itself guarantee that real-world data is correct?
  • It only proves data was recorded unchanged, not that it was true when entered (correct)
  • Because blocks are too small
  • Because miners lie
  • Because hashes are weak

That is the oracle problem.

Check what you just learned

1. An 'oracle' in blockchain terms is:
  • A fortune teller
  • A source that brings real-world data to a smart contract (correct)
  • A miner
  • A wallet

The chain needs inputs it can trust.
keyPoints: Blockchains cannot verify real-world truth by themselves.
Immutability, scale, cost and law all create trade-offs.

topics.title: Judging a claim
topics.html:
Signs of a strong project
SignWhy it matters

modules.summary: Protecting yourself, understanding the rules and choosing a path into the field.
modules.outcome: You can protect a wallet, spot common scams, understand why regulation matters and plan what to learn next.
modules.intro: The same properties that make blockchains powerful make mistakes expensive: transactions are final and nobody can reverse them for you. This last module is about staying safe, staying legal and choosing where to go next.

topics.title: Wallet and account safety
topics.html:
The essentials

  1. Back up the recovery phrase on paper, offline, in more than one safe place.
  2. Never type the recovery phrase into a website or share it in a message.
  3. Use a hardware wallet for amounts that matter.
  4. Use a separate wallet for experiments, with small amounts.
  5. Check addresses character by character, at least the start and end.
  6. Keep your phone and computer updated, and use two-step verification on exchange accounts.
  7. Revoke old permissions that apps hold over your tokens when you stop using them.
Common attacks
AttackHow it worksDefence
Phishing sitesA fake site copies a real one and asks you to connect and signBookmark the real site; read every signature request
Fake supportSomeone pretends to be support and asks for secretsSupport never needs your phrase
Address poisoningA look-alike address appears in your historyCopy addresses from a trusted source, not your recent list
Malicious approvalsYou approve a contract to move your tokensApprove only what is needed; review and revoke
Rug pullDevelopers drain a project's funds and disappearBe careful with new, unaudited tokens

Check what you just learned

1. Who legitimately needs your recovery phrase?
  • Nobody (correct)
  • An exchange helper
  • Support staff
  • Your friend

It should never be shared.

Watch out

If you think you have been scammed, stop sending money, collect the evidence, report it to the platform and to the cybercrime authority in your country, and be wary of 'recovery services' that ask for upfront fees; they are often a second scam.

Check what you just learned

1. A safe place for a recovery phrase is:
  • A screenshot in your photos
  • Written on paper and stored offline (correct)
  • An email draft
  • A chat message to yourself

Offline storage defeats online theft.
keyPoints: Protect the recovery phrase above all.
Phishing, fake support and malicious approvals are the main threats.

topics.title: Law, tax and responsibility
topics.html:
Rules about crypto assets differ widely and change often. In some countries they are heavily regulated, in others partly or not clearly regulated. A responsible learner checks the rules where they live before buying, selling or building.

Areas to check
AreaQuestion
TaxesAre gains, income or transfers taxed, and how must they be reported?
Consumer protectionWhich exchanges are licensed? What happens if one fails?
Financial regulationDoes a particular token count as a security or a regulated product?
Anti-money-laundering rulesWhat identity checks apply?
Data protectionCan personal data be put on a chain?
Employment and contractsWho is responsible when a smart contract fails?

Good habits

  • Keep records of your transactions, with dates and amounts.
  • Use licensed, well-known platforms where you can.
  • Do not use crypto to hide income or avoid taxes.
  • If you build something, take legal advice before launching a token or taking public money.
Watch out

This course gives general education, not legal, tax or investment advice. Ask a qualified professional in your country.

Check what you just learned

1. Why keep records of your crypto transactions?
  • For fun
  • Wallets delete them
  • Tax and legal rules may require them (correct)
  • Nobody needs them

Many places tax crypto activity.

Check what you just learned

1. The best response to unclear crypto rules is to:
  • Ignore them
  • Guess
  • Copy another country
  • Check local rules and ask a professional (correct)

Responsibility is yours.
keyPoints: Rules vary by country and change; check them.
This course is not legal, tax or investment advice.

Roles in the field

  • Smart contract developer
  • Web3 front-end or back-end developer
  • Security researcher and auditor
  • Product manager for a blockchain product
  • Data analyst for on-chain data
  • Compliance and risk specialist
  • Community and education roles

The best way to learn is to build small things, read other people's code and explain what you learned. Keep a notebook of terms and a list of projects you could try.

Tip

Follow the documentation of the chains you care about and read the post-mortems of failed projects. They teach more than success stories.

Practice and primary sources beat hype.

  • Rumours

They explain what went wrong.
